stages.P1: Population answer distributions: what real people (and which segments) say about a product or category
stages.P2: Initial perception and preference on first exposure, before use, across product and competitors
stages.P3: Task outcomes and preference after attempting given tasks on the product and competitors
stages.P4: Overall choice: which product people pick (primary target; brand and network effects excluded)

competing_alts.label: Competing alternatives
competing_alts.desc: People choose between real competing products or variants

brand_neutral.label: Brand-neutral
brand_neutral.desc: Blind comparison, unknown makers, or variants of one brand

who_attrs.label: Who they are
who_attrs.desc: Person-level attributes with enough people per segment

startup_realism.label: Startup realism
startup_realism.desc: Products are digital products comparable to a startup's

no_contam.label: Not memorized
no_contam.desc: A language model cannot already know the outcome

why.label: Reasons
why.desc: Multi-dimension ratings, rationales or free text

evaluable.label: Evaluable
evaluable.desc: Held-out splits, sample size, measurable noise ceiling

license.label: Publishable
license.desc: Public and publishable licence or terms

mcp_arm.label: Fair MCP arm
mcp_arm.desc: Non-target evidence exists that a tool-augmented model may use without leaking the answer

status.restricted: Restricted: on request, data deal, or non-commercial terms
status.proposed: Proposed: needs a pipeline or new data collection

benchmarks.name: HUMAINE

P1.why: Rating distributions (goal achievement, engagement 1-5) by demographic group; not questionnaire answers

P3.why: People do their own tasks with two AI assistants; goal achievement scored per conversation, then they compare

P4.why: Overall winner between competing products, per person, with age, ethnicity, politics, country

unverified: brand_neutral: whether models were anonymous to participants
benchmarks.note: 23k+ people, 22 demographic groups, US/UK. Products are AI assistants, not startup apps; models' reputations are known to LLMs.

benchmarks.name: PRISM

P1.why: Profile survey of 1,500 people (75 countries) with stated preferences about AI: category-level answer distributions by segment

P2.why: First-turn ratings of several models before choosing which to continue with

P3.why: Multi-turn conversations, but no task-completion score

P4.why: Per-conversation choice; no overall adoption decision

benchmarks.note: 8,011 conversations with 21 LLMs; rich individual profiles; skews young, white, educated.

benchmarks.name: Chatbot Arena votes

P3.why: Own prompts, usually single turn; no completion score

P4.why: Blind pairwise votes between competing products

benchmarks.note: Huge volume, no demographics; leaderboard widely published, so outcomes are known to LLMs.

benchmarks.name: Twin-2K-500

P1.why: 500 questions per person, 2,058 people, retest wave: person-level answer distributions

P2.why: Product description plus price, then buy or not

P4.why: Buy yes/no at a price; no choice against a competitor

benchmarks.note: Products are branded groceries (Land O Lakes, Tylenol). Adapter run: reasons pass, segments fail stability.

benchmarks.name: SimBench

P1.why: 20 datasets of real group answer distributions

benchmarks.note: Group level only; median 1-5 groups per question, so reasons and segments cannot be estimated. Our harness: 41.5 plain vs 55.8 with no target labels.

benchmarks.name: Pew ATP tech adoption
benchmarks.license: Free account; no resale or redistribution

P1.why: Person-level survey answers with full demographics, ~10k per wave

P4.why: Which platforms people actually use (big brands)

benchmarks.name: OPeRA

P3.why: Real shopping sessions: every action, purchase or abandon, with a rationale per step

benchmarks.note: Small (51 people, 692 sessions). Branded Amazon products.

benchmarks.name: ShopCART

P3.why: 31,865 Amazon sessions with actions and outcomes

benchmarks.note: No licence tag, so treat as restricted.

benchmarks.name: Online-Mind2Web

P3.why: Human task completion paths on real websites; no preference

benchmarks.note: Useful for task mechanics (branch 3), not for preference.

benchmarks.name: Upworthy A/B archive

P2.why: Headline variant clicks: first impression of a message

benchmarks.note: 32,487 randomized tests, aggregate clicks, news headlines 2013-15.

P2.why: Real UI A/B pairs with the winning variant from live tests

benchmarks.name: Show HN (live)

P2.why: Landing page first impression, captured at submission

P3.why: Some comments come from people who tried the product

benchmarks.note: Real startups, live so nothing to memorize; one audience, aggregate only. Needs the forecasting pipeline.

benchmarks.name: Product Hunt (live)

P4.why: Daily ranking among the day's launches

benchmarks.note: Needs permission; rankings carry campaign noise.

benchmarks.name: Kickstarter
benchmarks.license: public file lacks page text; text file restricted

P4.why: Backing with real money, among new unknown products

benchmarks.note: 610k projects 2009-2023; mostly physical and creative products.

P1.why: Appeal rating distributions by demographic and country

benchmarks.name: G2 / Capterra reviews
benchmarks.license: no scraping; needs a data deal

P3.why: Post-use ease of use, setup, support

P4.why: Alternatives considered and switched from, ratings against competitors

benchmarks.note: Closest to B2B software competitor choice, but not usable without a licence.

P4.why: Rating as a weak proxy for choice

benchmarks.name: UserSim own panel (target design)

P1.why: Profile survey of the same people

P2.why: First impression of product and competitors' pages

P3.why: The same people attempt the same tasks on each product

benchmarks.note: Not collected. Shown as the reference: the only design that links P1-P4 for the same people. Cost about $3-4k for 1,000 profiles plus each study.
